source_text: Verum haec loquimur, ut fidei vestrae quis sit finis ostendam; ceterum illud inconcussum valet, quod disputationibus praecedentibus fundatum est, nec quidquam malum esse, praeter opus voluntatis quod iustitia prohibet perpetrantis; nec quod naturale est, posse malum convinci. Manet ergo haec inconcussa turris, de cuius edito latrocinia diversorum propulsantur errorum.
pass_a_gloss: But we speak these things, that I may show what the end of your faith is; for the rest that avails unshaken which was founded by preceding disputations, that nothing is evil besides a work of will which justice forbids the perpetrator; nor can what is natural be convicted evil. This unshaken tower therefore remains, from whose height the robberies of diverse errors are driven back.

lemmas.lexica: LS naturalis; Blaise malum naturale=evil as a nature
LS voluntas=will, wish; Blaise moral will
LS/Blaise natura=created constitution, not 'original sin' itself
LS malum; Blaise malum naturale vs malum voluntatis

pass_b_english: But we speak this way to show where your creed ends. The point founded by the preceding discussions remains unshaken: nothing is evil except the act of a will committing what justice forbids; nor can what is natural be proved evil. This tower therefore stands unshaken, and from its height the brigandage of different errors is repelled.

choices.why: Julian's definition of sin is an act of will. Keep 'will' rather than later 'free will' system language unless liberum arbitrium is present.
Julian's Manichaean charge: an evil that is a nature, not a will's act.
Julian's charge against Augustine: treating evil as a nature rather than as will.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
